feature: The grid you set is the grid you see
summary: The grid chip in the tool bar now reads what the lines on screen are actually worth, not just the number you typed: at 100% a 4 pt grid reads "4 → 32 pt", because 32 is what is drawn and what a drag lands on. Zoom in and the two numbers become one again.
setup: Photonz Dev, Experiments window, release Next. The canvas grid flag is on by default. Any document will do.

try.do: Open any picture and press Command apostrophe to show the grid.
Read the grid chip in the tool bar, left of the zoom. At 100% it says 4 → 32 pt.
Press the chip and read the line under the Spacing field.
Press Escape, then zoom to 400%. The chip settles to 4 pt and the line under Spacing is gone.
Zoom out to 25%. The chip reads 4 → 256 pt, which is the spacing of the lines you can count.
Drag a layer at each zoom and check it lands on the number the chip is showing on the right of the arrow.
Turn Snap to grid off and watch the chip: the numbers do not move, only the mention of a drag leaves the line under Spacing.

evaluate: Reading the chip cold, is it obvious that 4 is what you set and 32 is what you are looking at?
Is the arrow the right way round, or would you rather see the live number first?
Is the second line under Spacing worth the two lines it takes, or is the chip enough on its own?
Does the chip changing as you zoom feel informative or restless?
Would you rather the app simply refused to keep a 4 pt grid it cannot draw, and said so once?
rough: The chip is 18pt wider than it was, so it needs the same canvas width the zoom slider does. Nothing else in the bar moved.

The task also offered drawing the set spacing faintly below the readable floor. That was not built: at 100% a 4 pt grid is 4 screen points apart, which is the grey wash the level of detail ladder exists to prevent.
Screen Recording was granted for this run, so both pictures here are real window captures, not offscreen renders.
